Who are we?
Some young people don't need to be made to fit school. They need a school designed to fit how they learn.
Forest Schooling UK provides specialist SEMH education for young people who need something different from a conventional classroom.
Through Berrylands School and our established Alternative Provision, we combine relationships, outdoor learning, therapeutic practice and personalised education to help young people reconnect with learning.​​
Learning beyond four walls
Education that changes lives
A genuine partnership with families

Home–School Partnership Agreement
Berrylands School
At Berrylands School, we recognise that many of our young people have experienced significant challenges in education before reaching us. For some, school has been associated with failure, anxiety, exclusion, conflict or simply feeling that they do not belong.
We believe that cycle can be broken.
Our aim is for every young person to rebuild trust in education, experience success and develop the confidence and skills they need for their future.
We cannot achieve this through school alone. It requires a strong and consistent partnership between the young person, their family and the school.
This agreement sets out the expectations that make that partnership work.
Respect and Communication
We expect all communication between home and school to be respectful.
Our staff will treat parents and carers with courtesy and respect, and we expect the same in return. Staff should not be shouted at, sworn at, threatened or spoken to aggressively, whether in person, by telephone, email or any other form of communication.
There will inevitably be occasions when parents or carers disagree with us. We welcome appropriate challenge and discussion. Disagreement, however, does not remove the expectation of respectful communication.
Parents and carers should read information provided through Arbor and the Daily Tracker before contacting the school about an incident or concern. This ensures conversations begin with the information already available.
Mobile Phones
Young people are expected to hand in their mobile phones on arrival at school. Phones will be stored securely and returned at the appropriate time.
Parents and carers should not contact their child directly on their mobile phone during the school day.
If a message needs to be passed to a young person, parents and carers should contact the school office. We will ensure that appropriate messages are passed on.
This allows young people to engage with school without the distraction or pressure of outside communication during the school day.
Attendance and Punctuality
Regular attendance is fundamental to making progress.
Young people are expected to attend school every day that they are required to attend, arrive on time and remain for their agreed timetable unless an absence has been authorised.
We recognise that some of our young people have previously struggled significantly with attendance. Where necessary, we will work with families to rebuild attendance carefully and sustainably.
However, once an attendance programme or timetable has been agreed, we expect home and school to work together to maintain it.
Unauthorised or purposeful absence will be addressed and, where appropriate, managed in conjunction with the relevant Education Welfare Service and Local Authority.
Learning
Berrylands is different from many schools our young people have previously experienced, but it is still a school.
We expect every young person to engage with learning at a level appropriate to their needs, ability and stage of development.
For some young people, progress may initially mean sitting with an adult for ten minutes, completing a short task or returning to learning after becoming dysregulated. For others, expectations will include sustained academic work and qualifications.
We will challenge our young people, but we will also remember the educational journey that brought them to us.
Small steps are still progress.
Parents and carers are expected to support the school's learning expectations and reinforce the importance of participation, effort and perseverance at home.
Working in Unison
One of the most important things we can give a young person is consistency.
Young people need to see that home and school are working together, not against each other.
There may be occasions when parents or carers disagree with a decision we have made. We will listen and discuss concerns respectfully. However, disagreements between adults should be dealt with between adults and should not undermine expectations or relationships in front of the young person.
Likewise, the school will listen carefully to parents and carers. You know your child in ways that we do not, and your knowledge is important to us.
Our young people need the adults around them to communicate, share information and present a consistent message.
Our Commitment
In return, Berrylands School commits to:
treat every young person and family with dignity and respect;
provide a safe, relational and supportive environment;
communicate openly and honestly with parents and carers;
recognise individual needs and circumstances;
celebrate progress, including the small steps;
challenge young people appropriately while recognising their previous experiences of education;
listen when things are not working and make reasonable adjustments where appropriate; and
continue to believe in a young person's potential, including when things are difficult.
Our Shared Commitment
Many of our young people arrive at Berrylands because previous educational experiences have not worked for them.
We have an opportunity to change that story.
Breaking the cycle will take patience, consistency, boundaries, trust and sometimes difficult conversations. There will be good days and difficult days. What matters is that the adults remain united around the young person.
School, home and the young person each have a part to play. When we work together, we give them the best possible opportunity to succeed.
Supporting Conversations at Home
A Practical Guide for Parents and Carers
Young people will naturally tell parents and carers about their school day from their own perspective. We want them to do this. They need to know that the adults at home will listen when something has upset, worried or angered them.
Listening, however, does not mean immediately reaching a conclusion about what has happened.
Our young people are developing the skills to understand situations, recognise their own part in events and see things from another person's perspective. Home and school need to help them develop these skills together.
We therefore ask parents and carers to listen first, check the Daily Tracker, understand the wider picture and then respond calmly.
“Someone hit me today.”
Parent/Carer: “That sounds serious. Let me read the tracker so I understand what happened, then we can talk about the facts together.”
“The staff were horrible to me.”
Parent/Carer: “I'm sorry you had a difficult day. Tell me what happened. I'll also read what school has recorded so we can understand the whole situation.”
“A member of staff shouted at me for no reason.”
Parent/Carer: “Okay. I want to hear your side. There may also be more to what happened, so let's look at the tracker together before we decide what we think.”
“I'm not going to school tomorrow.”
Parent/Carer: “I understand today was difficult, but not going isn't the answer. You are going to school tomorrow and we'll work with school to sort out what happened.”
“I don't want to go in tomorrow. I'm staying at home.”
Parent/Carer: “I hear that you don't want to go, and we can talk about why. But staying at home isn't the solution. School is expecting you tomorrow and I am expecting you to attend. If something needs sorting out, we will sort it out with school together.”
“The work is stupid. I'm not doing it.”
Parent/Carer: “You don't have to enjoy every piece of work, but you do have to try. School will support you, and I expect you to work with them.”
“They took my phone off me.”
Parent/Carer: “That's the school rule and we support it. If I need you during the day, I'll contact the office.”
“I got sent home and it wasn't my fault.”
Parent/Carer: “I'll listen to what you have to say and I'll read the school's account as well. Then we can talk about what happened and what needs to be different tomorrow.”
“Everyone at school is against me.”
Parent/Carer: “It might feel like that right now, but the adults at school are there to help you succeed. Let's work out what happened rather than deciding everyone is against you.”
“Tell them they can't make me do that.”
Parent/Carer: “If I disagree with something, I'll speak to the school about it. You don't need to fight that battle. Your job is to work with the adults and make good choices.”
“Can you ring school and tell them off?”
Parent/Carer: “If there's something I need to discuss with school, I will. But first I'm going to read the tracker and understand what happened. We're going to deal with this calmly.”
Listen. Check. Understand. Respond.
We can acknowledge how something felt to a young person without immediately assuming that their understanding of everything that happened is complete.
This does not mean dismissing a young person's concerns. It means taking them seriously enough to establish what happened before reaching conclusions. Listen to your child. Check the information. Understand the wider picture. Then respond.
Most importantly, let your child see that home and school are working together, not against each other.

About Our School Curriculum
Our approach focuses on strong relationships, emotional regulation and personalised pathways that help young people re-engage with learning and rebuild confidence.
Our curriculum is a young person-centred, therapeutic programme for those unable to access mainstream education due to SEMH needs. It blends trauma-informed practice, outdoor learning principles and individualised education to support cognitive, emotional, social and mental health development in a safe, nurturing environment.
It's Unique
Forest Schooling UK provides therapeutic, trauma-informed and nature-based pathways.
Our curriculum is built around our three core pathways, Roots, Nurture and Growth, and underpinned by our 8C’s Curriculum Framework.
At Forest Schooling UK, we do not group pupils by age or academic ability. Instead, we organise learning groups based on individual interests, strengths and emotional readiness.
This flexible approach allows young people to engage in meaningful, relevant activities that spark curiosity and build confidence. By focusing on interest-led learning rather than traditional year groups, we create a more inclusive and supportive environment where every child can thrive at their own pace.
Schemes of work include: English, Maths, Science, Information Technology, Geography & History, PE & Outdoors, Aesthetics and Creative Arts, PHSE
Young people learn best when they feel emotionally safe, confident and settled. That belief sits at the heart of our practice. Our curriculum is guided by the 8 C’s:
These principles are embedded across everything we do, shaping how young people think, learn, manage emotions, work with others and understand their place in the world.
Together, the 8 C’s support academic learning, personal development and resilience, helping young people grow into capable, reflective and responsible individuals.
All young people begin on our Roots Pathway, where they are introduced to the 8 C’s curriculum. This pathway aligns with EYFS principles, focusing on emotional security, confidence and readiness to learn.
We start by helping young people feel safe and settled, building strong relationships, consistent routines and personalised plans that allow learning to happen at the right pace. Respect, inclusion and emotional wellbeing are central, with every young person’s voice and journey valued.
As confidence develops, young people take increasing responsibility for their learning through the 8 C’s framework.
Academic learning is fully integrated and meaningful. English, Maths, Science, Computing, Humanities, PE, Creative Arts and PSHE are woven naturally into daily experiences through storytelling, exploration, movement and emotional literacy. Learning is practical, purposeful and designed to support both personal development and academic progress.
In the Nurture Phase, young people grow in confidence as they feel emotionally safe, valued and ready to engage with gentle, purposeful learning. Light academic demands are introduced at the right time, including reading, writing and exploring topics that spark genuine interest.
Through the 8 C’s, young people develop self-expression, emotional regulation, collaboration and independence. Curiosity and creativity drive learning, while composure, respect and compassion support positive relationships and thoughtful choices.
As confidence builds, learners may access the AQA Unit Award Scheme, allowing small but meaningful achievements to be formally recognised and progress to be personalised.
Academic learning is fully integrated into practical, real-world experiences, making it purposeful, relational and emotionally safe, supporting both personal development and academic engagement.
When a young person is fully settled and confident, they move into the Growth Phase. This stage introduces more sustained learning and higher expectations, while still respecting individual needs, strengths and pace.
With the 8 C’s securely embedded, learners begin to explore subjects in greater depth. Curiosity becomes focused, thinking more analytical, communication more purposeful and responsibility more explicit through goal-setting and follow-through. Engagement extends beyond the individual to the wider community.
At this stage, young people begin working towards formal qualifications suited to their interests and abilities. This may include Functional Skills, King’s Trust programmes, GCSEs, BTECs, project-based learning or supported apprenticeships that lead to real-world outcomes and progression.
Learning is increasingly applied and purposeful, with academic subjects embedded through extended projects, leadership opportunities and life-skills development. The focus shifts from re-engagement to independence, supporting young people to grow into confident, capable and contributing citizens.
It's Child Led
During the Growth Phase, one young person set himself a clear goal: to design a website reselling pre-owned games. What started as an interest quickly became a meaningful project.
Using skills developed through the 8 C’s, he designed and published a functional website, researched wholesale pricing, calculated costs and profits, and worked out realistic pricing models. He applied Maths through budgeting and profit margins, English through written content and product descriptions, and Computing through website design and digital publishing.
Beyond the technical skills, the project showed growing responsibility, composure and citizenship. His motivation wasn’t just personal, he hopes to use any profit to fund a cinema trip for the rest of his cohort.
This project reflects what the Growth Phase is about: purposeful learning, real-world application and young people using their skills to create positive outcomes for themselves and others.

Welcome to Forest Schooling UK
Forest Schooling UK provides education for young people aged 7–16 with Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH) needs who have often experienced disrupted schooling, exclusion or early trauma. For many, mainstream education hasn’t just been ineffective, it’s been the wrong environment altogether.
Based in Kingston, our work centres around Berrylands School, a full-time special school where learning happens predominantly outdoors, without a main school building. Education takes place in natural spaces, shepherds’ huts and small purpose-built structures, intentionally designed not to feel like conventional school. The setting is also genuinely off-grid, with water carried in and electricity generated on site through solar power.
Most young people progress into the school through our alternative provision, allowing trusted relationships with staff to be built early and carried through. Our flexible curriculum is paced to the young person, not the system, with pathways that include apprenticeships, vocational routes and GCSEs, all taken at the right time.
Forest Schooling UK exists because mainstream isn’t right for everyone. We offer a different kind of education, one built around relationships, readiness and real progress.
Our Story
Our Forest School began with a simple idea and a strong sense of purpose. One Wednesday afternoon, we opened a two-hour session in nature, not as a recreational outdoor activity, but as a safe, supportive space for children who needed something different. It quickly became clear that this wasn’t a nice extra; it was a necessity.

Welcome to Forest Schooling UK
A guide for our new starters
Starting somewhere new can feel exciting, confusing and maybe even a little scary. Lots of the young people who join us tell us they were worried before their first day, but they soon discover that Forest Schooling UK is a little different.
You don't have to be perfect. You don't have to know anyone before you arrive. You just have to come as you are.
We'll get to know you, help you settle in and make sure you feel welcome from day one.
What is it like?
Our days look a little different from many schools. You'll spend time outdoors, learn in small groups, explore the woods, look after animals, cook over the fire, build things, learn new skills and, of course, continue with your education.
Some days you'll be in the classroom.
Some days you'll be outside.
Every day you'll be supported by adults who genuinely care about helping you succeed.
Everyone is Different
You don't have to pretend to be someone you're not.
Some young people arrive feeling nervous.
Some have had a difficult time at previous schools.
Some love being outdoors.
Some have never tried Forest School before.
Wherever you're starting from, we'll meet you there.
What Should I Bring?
Bring clothes that you're happy to get muddy, sturdy shoes or boots and a waterproof coat. We spend lots of time outside, whatever the weather, because that's where some of the best learning happens! Don't worry if you forget something, we'll always do our best to help.
What Will My First Day Be Like?
When you arrive, one of our team will welcome you and show you around. You'll meet the adults you'll be working with and have plenty of time to explore. We know starting somewhere new can feel overwhelming, so there's no pressure to know everything straight away. We'll take things at your pace.
Take a Look Around
The photographs below show some of the places you'll see, the activities you'll take part in and some of the animals you might meet. We hope they help you feel a little more familiar with Forest Schooling UK before your first day. We can't wait to welcome you.
A few things we'd like you to remember...
You don't have to get everything right on your first day.
It's okay if you've never been to Forest School before.
Everyone deserves a fresh start.
If you're worried about anything, tell us, we'll always listen.
We believe in you, even before you believe in yourself.​
You don't need to change to belong here. We can't wait to get to know the real you.

Behaviour at Our Settings
Understanding Behaviour
Every young person arrives with a unique story. Their experiences, relationships, challenges, and strengths all shape how they communicate with the world around them. Because of this, we recognise that the point at which behaviour becomes concerning, the “red line” can look different for each young person depending on their individual journey.
Our role is not simply to enforce rules, but to understand the meaning behind behaviour and support young people to develop safer, healthier ways of expressing themselves.
Behaviour is Communication
We work from the understanding that behaviour is a form of communication. When a young person feels overwhelmed, anxious, angry, or unsafe, they may not yet have the language or emotional regulation skills to explain those feelings clearly. Behaviour can become the way those emotions are expressed.
For some young people, this may show itself through withdrawal or disengagement. For others, it may appear as frustration, strong language, or refusal to participate. In some cases, behaviour may escalate because the young person does not yet know another way to communicate how they are feeling.
Our focus is to look beyond the behaviour itself and ask an important question: “What is this young person trying to tell us?”
Expectations and the Moving Red Line
All young people deserve clear boundaries and consistent expectations. However, fairness does not always mean treating every young person exactly the same. It means understanding where a young person is in their development and supporting them to move forward.
For this reason, we recognise that the “red line” for behaviour may move as a young person grows, develops trust, and learns new ways to communicate. What matters most is progress over time. Our aim is to help each young person move steadily toward greater self-regulation, responsibility, and positive decision-making, supported by adults who understand their journey.
Language and Expression
Some young people we support have experienced environments where strong or inappropriate language was common. At times, this language may surface when a young person is frustrated or emotionally overwhelmed. Respectful communication remains an important expectation within our community.
However, it is not always realistic to expect perfect language at every moment for every young person, particularly when emotions are heightened.
When inappropriate language occurs, it is not ignored, but addressed calmly and constructively. Staff talk with the young person about the impact of their words, helping them reflect and develop more respectful ways to express themselves. These moments are treated as opportunities for learning rather than simply punishment. Over time, young people are supported to build greater awareness of their language and the effect it has on others.
Safety and Physical Behaviour
The safety of everyone in our community is essential. Violence towards others is not tolerated. At the same time, we recognise that for some young people who have experienced trauma or significant challenges, physical behaviour may sometimes be the only way they have learned to express distress, fear, or anger.
Rather than viewing this purely as defiance, we understand it as a signal that the young person needs support to regulate and communicate differently. Our response is always focused on safety first, followed by reflection, repair, and learning.
Skilled Staff and Relational Support
Our staff are highly trained in de-escalation, trauma informed relational approaches, and positive handling. This means they are equipped to recognise early signs of distress and respond in ways that help a young person calm, regulate, and regain control.
Through strong relationships and consistent support, staff can often help a young person pause, reflect, and make a better choice in the moment. Positive handling techniques are used only when absolutely necessary to keep everyone safe, and always in line with strict safeguarding procedures. Most importantly, our staff aim to create an environment where a young person feels understood, supported, and able to succeed.
Growth Over Perfection
We do not expect instant change, and we do not measure success by perfection. Instead, we focus on progress.
A young person who learns to pause before reacting, to express frustration with words rather than actions, or to repair a relationship after conflict has taken an important step forward.
Our goal is to help every young person develop the confidence, skills, and emotional awareness needed to navigate the world successfully, not just while they are with us, but long after they leave.

Safeguarding Our Young People
Safeguarding isn't just policy, it's at the heart of what we do.
At our Forest School, the safety, wellbeing, and protection of every young person is at the heart of everything we do. We are committed to creating a nurturing and secure environment where children feel safe to explore, take risks, and learn through nature-based experiences. Safeguarding is not just a policy, it is a core part of our culture and daily practice, and underpins our ethos of respect, trust, and care for every individual.
We recognise our duty of care to safeguard and promote the welfare of all young people in our setting. Our staff are fully trained in safeguarding procedures, child protection, and the Prevent Duty, which helps to protect children from the risks of radicalisation and extremism. We follow clear, robust policies and procedures that align with current statutory guidance, including Working Together to Safeguard Children and Keeping Children Safe in Education.
We take a proactive and preventative approach, aiming to identify concerns early and respond swiftly and appropriately. Our young people's voices are valued and listened to, and we foster an open, supportive environment where they feel empowered to speak up and seek help if needed.
To ensure a holistic approach to safeguarding, we work closely with a range of professional services, including social care, health professionals, police, education authorities, and local safeguarding partners. These collaborative relationships enable us to share concerns, seek expert guidance, and put in place timely support for young people and families.
By embedding strong safeguarding practices and fulfilling our responsibilities under the Prevent Duty, we are committed to providing a Forest School experience where every young person can thrive, feel safe, and grow with confidence.
Berrylands School is proud to be part of Operation Encompass, a national safeguarding initiative that helps schools provide timely support to children who may have been affected by domestic abuse. Through this partnership, the police notify our Designated Safeguarding Lead before the start of the school day if a child has been present during a domestic abuse incident. This enables us to offer appropriate care, understanding and support, ensuring every child feels safe, valued and ready to learn.​
‘Working Together to Safeguard Children’ is a guide for all the different people
who should work together if you need help. It explains what is expected of them, and what they have to do to make sure you are listened to. It also tells them how they can help you understand what help and support you can get.
This version of the guide is made especially for children and young people. It was made because you have a right to know how the people who help you work with each other and what you can expect when you ask for help.
Our Safeguarding Leads
A safeguarding concern is any worry that a child or young person may be at risk of harm, abuse, neglect, exploitation, or unsafe treatment, whether this happens in school, at home, online, or in the community. If you notice something that doesn’t feel right, even if you are unsure, it is important to share it.
Concerns about our young people can be reported by emailing or calling one of our Designated Safeguarding Leads (DSLs) using the contact details below. All concerns will be treated seriously and handled confidentially in line with our safeguarding procedures.
If a child is in immediate danger, please contact emergency services.

British Values at Our School
At our school, we prepare young people to take an active, positive role in society. We promote the fundamental British values of democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, mutual respect, and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs through our core school values of Ready, Respectful & Responsible.
These values shape the way we learn, work, and live together as a school community. They guide how young people participate in decisions, treat one another, and develop the confidence to make thoughtful choices.
Democracy
Democracy means that everyone has a voice and that decisions are made fairly by listening to different views. We encourage young people to be Ready to share ideas and participate in discussions, while showing Respect by listening to the opinions of others. Through group learning, collaborative decision-making, and opportunities to contribute to school life, young people learn that their voice matters. With this voice comes Responsibility. young people that expressing an opinion also means considering the views and needs of others.
The Rule of Law
The rule of law helps communities remain safe, fair, and supportive for everyone. In our settings, young people are Ready to understand expectations and why rules are important. Our shared boundaries help everyone feel secure and able to learn. young people show Respect by following agreed expectations and recognising how their behaviour affects others. When difficulties arise, we encourage reflection and repair, helping young people take Responsibility for their actions and learn from them.
Individual Liberty
Individual liberty means having the freedom to make choices, express ideas, and develop as an individual. We encourage young people to be Ready to try new experiences, take safe risks in learning, and explore their interests. Young people are supported to develop confidence in their abilities and their voice. Alongside this freedom, young people learn to show Respect for the rights of others and take Responsibility for their choices, understanding how their actions contribute to the wellbeing of the whole community.
Mutual Respect
Mutual respect is central to our school culture. Young people are Ready to work together, share ideas, and support one another in learning. We actively encourage kindness, empathy, and positive relationships. Young people demonstrate Respect through their words and actions, recognising the value of every member of the community. They also take Responsibility for creating an environment where everyone feels safe, included, and valued.
Respect Different Faiths and Beliefs
We encourage young people to develop curiosity and understanding about the diverse world around them. young people are Ready to learn about different cultures, beliefs, and traditions through discussion, stories, and shared experiences. They show Respect by valuing differences and recognising that people may hold different perspectives.
Our young people learn to take Responsibility for building a community where everyone feels welcome and accepted, regardless of background, belief, or identity.​ Through our focus on Ready, Respectful & Responsible, we help pupils develop the character, confidence, and understanding needed to thrive both within school and in the wider world.

Our AP Referral Process Explained
Young people in Year R - Year 9 can only be considered for our Alternative Provision if they have a clear presenting need related to Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH). Our provision is specifically designed to support learners whose primary barriers to education are emotional regulation, behaviour, mental health, or social interaction. Without an SEMH presenting need, the support we offer would be inappropriate and ineffective, so referrals must clearly evidence SEMH as the main driver for placement.
Our Five Step Process
Referral Received
Our part-time Alternative Provision primarily supports young people in Years R-9 who are on roll with a named school. Referrals for those outside formal education, including EHE or SEMH-related placements are considered on a case-by-case basis.
We only accept referrals from our website forms found below.
Observation Offered
If the young person fits our criteria they will be offered an
observation placement. This allows us to assess fit,
support needs, and readiness. This is a short 20-30 minute process carried out at our site or the young persons current placement if appropriate.
Referral Review
We review: needs, suitability and capacity as a team. Please ensure you supply as much detail as you can on the referral form.
Decision Made
A decision is reached based on observation outcomes, individual needs, discussions with parents and the child's current placement as well as provision suitability.
Offer Made
A formal offer is issued where appropriate. Once accepted a
start date is arranged. You have 5 days in which to accept the offer.

Schools can refer children to our part-time SEMH Alternative Provision for up to three sessions per week. Schools fund this provision directly.
Any school can refer — an EHCP is not required.

Can I visit the provision before making a referral?
Due to the high number of referrals and enquiries we receive, we are unable to offer individual visits before a formal referral has been received and reviewed.
A referral must be submitted and accepted for consideration before a visit can be arranged. This helps us ensure that the young person meets our admissions criteria and that we are likely to be able to meet their needs before inviting families and professionals to visit.
We understand that choosing the right provision is an important decision, and we do not want to raise expectations or disappoint young people and families by arranging visits where a placement may not be appropriate or available.
Once we have reviewed a referral and believe we may be able to offer a suitable placement, we will be very happy to arrange a visit as part of the next stage of the process.
What type of young person is your provision suitable for?
We primarily support young people who are struggling to access or engage successfully with mainstream education. Many of our young people have SEMH needs, experienced trauma, anxiety, emotionally based school avoidance, difficulties with regulation or emerging additional needs.
Does a young person need an EHCP?
No. We support young people both with and without an EHCP. The referral and funding route will depend on the young person’s circumstances.
How long is a placement?
Our placements are designed as meaningful interventions rather than short-term respite. We generally require a minimum commitment of 19 weeks to allow relationships to develop and meaningful progress to be made.
How many days can a young person attend?
Most young people attend for one or two days per week, depending on their needs, the aims of the placement and availability. Our AP operates in sessions rather than as a replacement for a full-time school timetable.
Does the young person remain on their school roll?
In most cases, yes. The referring school remains responsible for the young person’s overall education and statutory responsibilities unless a different arrangement has been formally agreed.
What does a typical session involve?
Sessions combine outdoor learning, practical activities, relationship-building, emotional regulation and personalised learning opportunities. Our approach is deliberately flexible and responds to the needs and interests of each group.
Is this a behaviour provision?
Yes! We support young people whose behaviour may communicate significant unmet needs, but we are not simply a provision for removing disruptive pupils from school. Referrals must have clear outcomes and the placement must be appropriate for both the individual and the existing group.
Can you support young people with challenging behaviour?
Yes, where we believe we can safely and effectively meet their needs. We consider the nature, frequency and severity of behaviours alongside the needs of our existing cohort. Full and honest disclosure at referral is essential.
What information do you need before accepting a referral?
We require comprehensive and up-to-date information, including relevant safeguarding information, behaviour and risk information, attendance, SEND needs, EHCP documentation where applicable, current professional involvement and the reasons for referral. Failure to disclose significant information may result in a placement being reviewed or withdrawn.
How do you decide whether a placement is suitable?
We consider the young person’s needs, risks, desired outcomes and presentation alongside the dynamics of the proposed group. Being able to offer a space does not automatically mean that the placement is suitable.
How do you communicate with the referring school or professional?
We maintain regular communication with referrers and share relevant information about safeguarding, attendance, progress and significant incidents. We do this vis email and telephone. We also contribute to professional meetings, reports and reviews where appropriate.
Can attending your AP lead to a place at Berrylands School?
Potentially, but attendance at our AP does not guarantee admission to Berrylands School. Young people must normally have attended our AP for at least 19 weeks before we would consider whether a consultation to Berrylands School may be appropriate. Admission to the school is subject to separate criteria, suitability, availability and the formal local authority consultation process.
What makes Forest Schooling UK different?
We are an outdoors-first, relational and trauma-informed provision. We work with young people who often need something fundamentally different from a traditional classroom environment. Our small groups, consistent adults and practical approach give young people the space to regulate, build trust and reconnect with learning.

Attendance
​Regular attendance is fundamental to a young person’s progress with us because meaningful change, trust, and learning can only develop through consistent connection and shared experience. Each day builds on the last: relationships deepen, confidence grows, routines become secure, and small successes begin to compound into lasting personal development.
When attendance is irregular, this continuity is broken, making it far harder for young people to feel safe, regulate their emotions and engage fully in the opportunities around them. Simply put, the more present a young person is, the more they are able to benefit from the support of adults, the stability of structure, and the restorative power of time spent learning, connecting, and growing within our community.

Berrylands School Referral Process Explained
Young people aged 7–16 may only be considered for referral to Berrylands School if they are already known to us through our Alternative Provision (AP) and have a clear presenting need relating to Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH).
Our provision is specifically designed to support young people whose primary barriers to education relate to emotional regulation, behaviour, mental health, trauma, or social interaction.
​We work closely with Achieving for Children and accept referrals through the local authority pathway ONLY. In most cases, young people referred to us will already have an allocated caseworker, be in our AP and be progressing through, or already known to, the EHCP pathway.
Referrals that do not evidence an established SEMH need and prior engagement through our AP will not be considered.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ's)
What subjects are included in the curriculum?
Our curriculum includes a mix of academic subjects, creative arts, and outdoor activities, all designed to support the holistic development of our students.
What happens before a young person is offered a place at the AP?
Young people are usually known to us through our Alternative Provision first. This allows us to build relationships, assess suitability and ensure that Berrylands School is the right environment before any transition into full-time education is considered.
Who we are?
Forest Schooling UK has been delivering provision at St John’s School in Kingston upon Thames for several years. In addition, we operate across two further sites in Berrylands, Kingston. We accept referrals through the Education Inclusion Support Service (EISS) at Achieving for Children, as well as direct referrals from schools and home-educating families of children with Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH) needs.
Our team is made up of highly trained Forest School Leaders and experienced support staff, all skilled in working with young people who present with challenging behaviours. Every member of staff receives annual safeguarding training and is qualified in specialist outdoor first aid. You can find out more about our team here.
Where are we?
FSUK has sites at St Johns Primary and Nursery School and Hogsmill Nature Reserve, both in Kingston Upon Thames. Our sites consists of allotments, forest areas and open spaces. We have small classrooms as most of our activity is outdoors. The sites are secure and have separate gates away from other young people and adults. We have running water and a compostable toilet. We all have radios for contacting each other if needed.
I am worried about the young person missing 'academic' lessons
We believe that a young person is not able to study in a conventional school setting until they are emotionally secure within themselves. We do not have 'learning objectives' and the entire session is young person focussed and led. We do however follow and believe in our 8 C's curriculum in our AP and try to ensure this is embedded if everything we do. Those in full time placements go onto Roots, Nurture & Growth following the 8C's Framework.

What should a young person wear for cold weather?
Base Layer
The children will be outside, so thermal leggings (long johns) with a thermal long-sleeved top. If you don’t have those and it’s not too cold, tights will do at a push.
Warm trousers – fleecy ones like jogging trousers or tracksuit bottoms.
A long-sleeved T-shirt or thin top.
A fleece sweater (preferably one that zips up).
Socks – a thin “normal” pair (like school socks, preferably cotton) and then a thick pair of ski, thermal or woolly socks.
Outer layer
A warm coat or jacket – one that doesn’t matter if it gets wet or muddy.
Snow boots or warm boots are better than wellies: wellington boots need a couple of pairs of socks inside on cold days, so be prepared to go up a size or two. Their ordinary wellies probably won’t be roomy enough for the warm layers.
Waterproofs – even more important in winter than in summer. Puddle suits or rain suits are perfect. For older children, waterproof trousers and a light waterproof jacket. Waterproof mittens can fit over woollen mittens for dry hands in wet weather.
Extra Kit
Use your judgement on really cold days: send your children to forest school with an extra jumper or base layer if it feels like that would be needed. They can always take layers off but it’s hard to get warm if you don’t have the right kit.
Spare gloves, spare socks and a change of trousers (in case they fall in the snow or water while not wearing waterproofs – it happens!).

What is the social challenge being targeted by your organisation?
traditional school settings—particularly those with Social, Emotional, and Mental Health (SEMH) needs, trauma histories, neurodiversity, or challenging life circumstances.
Across the UK, rising numbers of children are being excluded from mainstream education or disengaging entirely due to environments that are not equipped to meet their complex emotional and behavioural needs. Many of these children face cycles of isolation, low self-esteem and poor mental health, leading to long-term disadvantage and social marginalisation.
Our organisation targets this problem by offering an inclusive, therapeutic and nature-based alternative to conventional schooling. We provide safe, restorative spaces where children can rebuild trust in adults, regulate their emotions and re-engage with learning at their own pace—often for the first time. Our approach reduces the need for exclusion, supports earlier intervention and helps children develop the social and emotional foundations they need to succeed in life.
In doing so, Forest Schooling UK addresses wider social challenges such as:
Educational inequality
Youth mental health and well-being
Exclusion and off-rolling
Lack of appropriate support for neurodiverse learners
Barriers to inclusion in mainstream education
We believe that no child is “unreachable”—but many are simply being taught in ways that do not meet their needs. We aim to change that.
Our Social Mission
The mission of Forest Schooling UK is to transform the lives of children and young people who are struggling in traditional education by providing inclusive, restorative and nature-based learning experiences.
We are committed to creating safe, therapeutic outdoor environments where every child—particularly those with SEMH needs, neurodiversity, or trauma histories—can build confidence, develop emotional resilience and re-engage with learning in a way that respects their individuality and dignity.
Our work aims to reduce educational exclusion, promote mental well-being and champion a more compassionate, child-centred approach to education across the UK.

Impact & Outcomes
Forest Schooling UK was created to give children who have struggled elsewhere the opportunity to thrive. As a not-for-profit Community Interest Company, every pound we receive is reinvested into improving the education, wellbeing and opportunities of the young people we support. We believe success is measured not only by qualifications, but by confidence, attendance, resilience and brighter futures. This page shares the impact of our work and the outcomes our children achieve every day.
Case Studies
Luke
When Luke joined Forest Schooling UK's Alternative Provision, he was an exceptionally bright young person whose experiences outside of school had significantly impacted his ability to access education. Having witnessed domestic abuse and been supported through a Child Protection Plan,
Luke presented with high levels of anxiety and hypervigilance. In mainstream school, this often resulted in a flight-or-fight response, with incidents involving running from classrooms, climbing fences, refusing adult direction and, at times, becoming physically or verbally aggressive towards staff and peers. Despite his academic potential, he was frequently suspended and unable to access learning consistently.
Over the last 18 months, Luke has attended our Alternative Provision, where the emphasis has been on creating safety, building trusting relationships and helping him develop emotional regulation. During this time, he has also experienced two house moves, adding further instability to an already challenging childhood. Throughout these changes, Forest Schooling UK has provided one consistent, predictable environment where he has continued to attend, build relationships and feel a sense of belonging.
As Luke has grown in confidence, staff have seen a remarkable change. Although he still requires significant support and there are times when he becomes dysregulated, he is increasingly able to recognise when he needs support, accept help from trusted adults and recover from difficult moments more quickly. His curiosity, intelligence and sense of humour now shine through far more often than the behaviours that once defined his school experience.
This September, Luke will transition to Berrylands School, where he will continue his education with the adults and therapeutic approach he already knows and trusts. Rather than starting again in an unfamiliar environment, he will be able to build on the progress he has already made.
Luke's story is a reminder that behaviour is often a reflection of lived experiences rather than a child's potential. By providing consistency, understanding and a trauma-informed approach, we have helped him move from simply surviving each school day towards believing that education is somewhere he can succeed.
Simon
When Simon was referred to Forest Schooling UK, he was unable to consistently access mainstream education. His attendance had fallen to 30%, and even on a significantly reduced timetable he struggled to remain in the classroom for more than a few minutes before becoming overwhelmed by anxiety. Academically, he was working around four years below age-related expectations, particularly in reading, writing and mathematics.
Simon joined our Alternative Provision, where our initial focus was on building trust, reducing anxiety and helping him experience success again through our outdoor, trauma-informed approach. As his confidence grew, one of our team successfully supported him back into his mainstream school, accompanying him throughout the day. With a trusted adult alongside him, Simon accessed learning calmly and without the visible anxiety that had previously prevented him from attending.
Unfortunately, when this support was no longer available, Simon's ability to access mainstream education declined again.
Rather than forcing a placement that was no longer meeting his needs, he continued attending our Alternative Provision while the local authority sought a specialist setting. During this time, he continued to make steady progress emotionally, socially and academically.
Today, Simon is a pupil at Berrylands School, where he is thriving. His attendance has increased dramatically from 30% to 92%, reflecting the impact of being in the right environment with consistent relationships and specialist support. He is making excellent progress with his reading, is fully engaged in learning and approaches new experiences with confidence and enthusiasm.
Beyond the classroom, Simon has become an important member of our school community. He has proudly worked alongside staff helping to build our shepherd's huts and furniture, developing practical skills, resilience and a genuine sense of ownership in his school. Simon has made friends and has regular playdates, something that didn't happen in his old setting.
Simon's journey shows what is possible when a child is supported in an environment that understands their needs. With the right relationships, personalised support and an education built around strengths rather than barriers, he has rediscovered a love of learning and is now achieving both academically and personally.
